For $0 \lt t \lt 2s$ current varies linearly with time and given as $i(t)=3t$ and for $2s \lt t \lt 4s$ current is constant, $i(t)=6A$.

The energy absorbed by the inductor (Resistance neglected) in the first 2 sec,

$E_L=\int_{0}^{T}Li\frac{di}{dt}=E_{L_1}+E_{L_2}$

$E_{L_1}=\int_{0}^{2}Li \left (\frac{di}{dt} \right )dt$

$\;\;=\int_{0}^{2} 2 \times 3t \times 3\; dt$

$\;\;=18\int_{0}^{2}t\; dt$

$$\;\;=18 \times \left.\begin{matrix} \frac{t^2}{2} \end{matrix}\right|^2_0$$

$\;\;= 18 \times \left [ \frac{4}{2}-0 \right ]=36J$

The energy absorbed by the inductor in ($2\rightarrow 4$) second

$E_{L_2}=\int_{2}^{4}Li\left ( \frac{di}{dt}dt \right )$

$\;\;=\frac{2}{4}2 \times 6 \times 0 \;dt=0 J$

A pure indictor does not dissipate enegy but only stores it. Due to resistance, some energy is dissipated in the resistor. Therefore, total energy stored in the inductor and the energy dissipated in the resistor.

The energy dissipated by the resistance in 4 sec.

$E_R=\int_{0}^{T}i^2 R\;dt$

$\;\;=\int_{0}^{2}(3t)^2 \times 1 \;dt+\int_{2}^{4}6^2 \times 1 \; dt$

$\;\;=9\int_{0}^{2}t^2\;dt +36\int_{2}^{4}1 \; dt$

$$\;\;=9 \times \left.\begin{matrix} \frac{t^3}{3} \end{matrix}\right|_0^2+36t|_2^4$$

$\;\;=9 \times \left ( \frac{8}{3} \right )+36 \times 2$

$\;\;=24+72=96J$

The total energy absorbed by the inductor in 4 sec

$=96 J +36 J =132 J$

Therefore, the correct answer is **C**.

$$\begin{aligned} V &\propto f\phi \\ &\text{in induction machine}\\ V_2&= \frac{V_1}{2}\\ \text{and}\;\; f_2 &=\frac{f_1}{2} \\ \frac{V_1}{V_2} &=\frac{f_1\phi _1}{f_2\phi _2} \\ \phi _2&= \left ( \frac{V_2}{V_1} \right )\left ( \frac{f_1}{f_2} \right )\phi _1\\ &= \left ( \frac{V_1/2}{V_1} \right )\left ( \frac{f_1}{f_1/2} \right )\phi _1\\ &= \phi _1 \end{aligned}$$

So, air-gap flux remains same.

$(X_2')_1=$ nominal rotor stanstill reactance referred to stator (at frequency $f_1$)

$$\begin{aligned} (X_2')_2 &= \left ( \frac{f_2}{f_1} \right )(X_2')_1\\ &= \left ( \frac{f_1/2}{f_1} \right )(X_2')_1\\ &= \frac{(X_2')_1}{2}\\ (\omega _s)_2 &= \left ( \frac{f_2}{f_1} \right ) (\omega _s)_1\\ &= \left ( \frac{f_1/2}{f_1} \right ) (\omega _s)_1\\ &=\frac{(\omega _s)_1}{2} \end{aligned}$$

Torque developed in induction motor

$T=\frac{3}{\omega _s} \frac{V^2R'_2/s}{(R'_2/s)^2 +{X'_2}^2}$

For normal steady state oprating region, slip is very low

$\frac{R'_2}{s} \gt \gt X'_2$

$T=\frac{3}{\omega _s} \frac{V^2R'_2/s}{(R'_2/s)^2}=\frac{3}{\omega _s} \frac{sV^2}{R'_2}$

As the load torque is constant

$$\begin{aligned} T_1 &=T_2 \\ \frac{s_1V_1^2}{(\omega _s)_1R'_2}&= \frac{s_2V_2^2}{(\omega _s)_2R'_2}\\ \Rightarrow \;\; s_2 &=\frac{(\omega _s)_2}{(\omega _s)_1} \times \left ( \frac{V_1}{V_2} \right )^2 s_1\\ &=\frac{(\omega _s)_1/2}{(\omega _s)_1} \times \left ( \frac{V_1}{V_1/2} \right )^2 s_1 \\ s_2 &= \frac{1}{2} \times 4 \times s_1=2s_1 \end{aligned}$$

Difference between synchronous speed and actual speed

$$\begin{aligned} \omega _s -\omega _r &= s\omega _s\\ (\omega _s)_1 -(\omega _r)_2 &= s_2(\omega _s)_2\\ &=(2s_1) \times \frac{(\omega _s)_1}{2} =s_1(\omega _s)_1 \end{aligned}$$

Therefore, the difference between synchronous speed and actual speed remain same.

Stator current

$$\begin{aligned} |I_s| &= \frac{V}{\sqrt{(R'_2/s)^2+{X'}_2^2}} \\ \text{as}\;\; R'_2/s & \gt \gt X'_2 \\ |I_s|&=\frac{sV}{R'_2} \\ |I_{s1}|&= s_1\frac{V_1}{R'_2}\\ |I_{s2}|&=s_2\frac{V_2}{R'_2} \\ ||I_{s2}&=(2s_1)\times \frac{V_1/2}{R'_2}=\frac{s_1V_1}{R'_2} \\ ||I_{s1}&=|I_{s2}| \end{aligned}$$

Therefore, stator current remains same.

Therefore, the correct answer is **B**.

when two voltages are in phase i.e. $[\phi =0^{\circ}\; \text{or} \;180^{\circ}]$, the trace is straight line. But for $\phi =0^{\circ}$, the trace has positive slope and $\phi =180^{\circ}$, the trace has negative slope.

When the two voltage has phase displacement of $\phi =90^{\circ}$, the trace is a circle. If the direction of the trace is in the clockwise direction then the phase difference is $\phi =90^{\circ}$.

When the difference is not equal to $0^{\circ}$ or $90^{\circ}$, the trace is an ellipse. For $\pi \leq \phi \leq \frac{3\pi}{2}$, the trace is an ellipse in anti-clockwise direction.

$$sI-A=\begin{bmatrix} s & 0\\ 0 & s \end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix} 0 &2 \\ 2& 0 \end{bmatrix}$$

$$\;\;\;=\begin{bmatrix} s &-2 \\ -2& s \end{bmatrix}$$

Characteristic equation $\Rightarrow |sI-A|=0$

$$\begin{bmatrix} s &-2 \\ -2& s \end{bmatrix}=0$$

$\Rightarrow \;\; s^2-4=0$

Roots of the characteristic equation are -2 and +2.

Therefore, the correct answer is **A**.

$G(s)=\frac{k}{s(s+2)}$ and $H(s)=1+sP$

Closed-loop transfer function,

$\;\;=\frac{\frac{k}{s(s+2)}}{1+\frac{k}{s(s+2)}\cdot (1+sP)}$

$\;\;=\frac{k}{s(s+2)+k(1+sP)}$

$\Rightarrow \; T(s)=\frac{k}{s^2+(2+kP)s+k}$

So, characteristic equation $= s^2+(2+kP)s+k$

Comparing with standard equation  $=s^2+2\xi \omega _n s+\omega _n^2$

$\;\;\; k=\omega _n^2=5^2=25$

(where $\omega _n =$ undamped natueal frequency)

$\;\; 2\xi \omega _n=2+kP$

$\Rightarrow \; 2 \times 0.7 \times 5=2+25P$

(where $\xi =$ damping ratio)

$P=0.2$

Therefore, the correct answer is **D**.

Corner frequencys

$\omega _1= 1$ rad/sec; $\omega _2= 10$ rad/sec and $\omega _3=100$ rad/sec

For frequency less than $\omega _1 \; i.e. \; \omega \lt \omega _1$

Gain of the system is constant aas there is no pole at origin.

Gain$=20 log k=20 log 0.1=-20 dB$

At $\omega =\omega _1= 1$ rad/sec or $\omega _1= log 1 =0$

There is zero, so system gain increases with slope +20dB/decades and system gain become 0 dB at $\omega = 10$ rad/sec or $log\omega |_{\omega =10}=log 10=1$

At $\omega _2 =10$ or $log \omega |_{\omega _2=10}=log 10=1$

there is pole, so slope is -20 dB/decade.

Overall slope $\omega _2 \lt \omega \lt \omega _3$

= 20 dB/decade - 20 dB/decade

= 0 dB/decade

$\omega _2 \lt \omega \lt\omega _3$

At $\omega =\omega _3 =100$ rad/sec or

the double pole are present.

$$\begin{aligned} T(j\omega )&=\frac{900}{j\omega (j\omega +1)(j\omega +9)} \\ \angle T(j\omega )&=-90^{\circ}-tan ^{-1}\omega -tan^{-1}\left ( \frac{\omega }{9} \right ) \\ \text{At, } & (\omega _{pc})_1,\angle T(j\omega )=-180^{\circ}\\ -180^{\circ}&=-90^{\circ}-tan^{-1}(\omega _{pc})_1 -tan^{-1}\left ( \frac{(\omega _{pc})_1}{9} \right )\\ -90^{\circ}&=tan^{-1}\frac{(\omega _{pc})_1+\frac{(\omega _{pc})_1}{9}}{1-\frac{(\omega _{pc})^2_1}{9}} \\ \Rightarrow 1-\frac{(\omega _{pc})^2_1}{9}&=0 \\ \Rightarrow (\omega _{pc})_1&= 3 \text{ rad/sec}   \end{aligned}$$

Gain cross frequency of compensated system, $(\omega _{gc})_2$= phase cross frequency of uncompensated system, $(\omega _{pc})_1$

$\Rightarrow \;\;(\omega _{gc})_2=(\omega _{gc})_1=\; 3$  rad/sec

Phase-margin   $=180^{\circ}+\angle T(j\omega )|_{\omega =(\omega _{gc})_2}$

Let X dB is the gain provided by the compensator, so at gain cross frequency, $|T(j\omega )|_{com}$=1 or 0 dB. Gain of uncompensated system $=|T(j\omega )|_{un-com} =\frac{100}{\omega \sqrt{1+\omega ^2}\sqrt{1+\left ( \frac{\omega }{9} \right )^2}}$

$\;=40-20 \log \omega -20 \log \sqrt{1+\omega ^2} -20 \log \sqrt{1+\left ( \frac{\omega }{9} \right )^2}$

Gain of compensated system,

$|T(j\omega )|_{com}=X+|T(j\omega )_{un-com}|$

$|T(j\omega )|_{com}$ must be zero at gain cross frequency $(\omega _{gc})_2$

$|T(j\omega_{gc} )_2|_{com}=X+40-20 \log (\omega _{gc})_2 -20 \log \sqrt{1+(\omega _{gc})^2_2}-20 \log \sqrt{1+\frac{(\omega _{gc})^2}{9^2}}=0$

Now, the eigen value problem is $[A-\lambda I]\hat{x}=0$

$$\begin{bmatrix} 1-\lambda &1 &0 \\ 0 & 2-\lambda & 2\\ 0& 0 &3-\lambda \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2\\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 0\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$$

Putting $\lambda _1=1$, we get the eigen vector corresponding to this eigen value,

$$\begin{bmatrix} 0&1 &0 \\ 0 & 1& 2\\ 0& 0 &2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2\\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 0\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$$

Which gives the equations

$$\begin{aligned} x_2&=0 \\ x_2+2x_3&=0 \\ 2x_3 &=0 \end{aligned}$$

The solution is $x_2=0, x_3=0, x_1=k$

So, one eigen vector is $$\hat{x_1}=\begin{bmatrix} k\\ 0\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}\;i.e.\; x_1:x_2:x_3=k:0:0$$

Since, none of the eigen vectors given in choises matches with this, ratio we need to proceed further and find the other eigen vectors corresponding to the other eigen values.

$$\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1\\ 4& -1 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0\\ 2& 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1\\ 0&-3 \end{bmatrix}$$

But this is not any of the choises given.

So let us do Crout's decomposition, by putting $u_{11}=1$ and $u_{22}=1$

$$\begin{aligned} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1\\ 4& -1 \end{bmatrix}&=\begin{bmatrix} l_{11} & 0\\ l_{21}& l_{22} \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & u_{12}\\ 0&1 \end{bmatrix} \\ l_{11} &=2,l_{11}u_{12} =1\\ \Rightarrow \; u_{12}&=\frac{1}{2}=0.5 \\ l_{21}&=4,l_{21}u_{12}+l_{22}=-1 \\ \Rightarrow \; 4 \times \frac{1}{2}+l_{22} &=-1 \\ \Rightarrow \;l_{22} &=-3 \\ So\;\; \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1\\ 4 &-1 \end{bmatrix} &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0\\ 4& -3 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0.5\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned}$$

Therefore, the correct answer is **D**.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Eddy current loss} &=P_{e1} \\ \text{Hysteresis loss}&=P_{h1} \\ V_2=138V &, f_230Hz \\ \text{Eddy current loss} &=P_{e2} \\ \text{Hysteresis loss}&=P_{h2} \\ \text{we know that, } & \\ \text{Eddy current loss,}\;& P_e \propto B_m^2f^2 \\ \text{and hysteresis loss,}&P_h \propto B_m^xf\propto B_m^1.6 f \\ &(\text{Typical value of x=1.6}) \end{aligned}$$

The transformer induced emf equation is:

$$\begin{aligned} V_1 &=\sqrt{2} \pi \phi _m N \\ V_1&= \sqrt{2} \pi f B_m A N\\ \text{where,}\;\; \frac{V}{t} &=\text{constant} \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \frac{P_{e2}}{P_{e1}} &=\left ( \frac{V_2}{V_1} \right )^2=\left ( \frac{138}{230} \right )^2=0.36 \\ \text{or,} \;\; P_{e2} &= 0.36P_{e1}\;\;...(i)\\ \text{Also,} \;\;\frac{P_{h2}}{P_{e1}} &=\left ( \frac{V_2}{V_1} \right )^{1.6} \times \left ( \frac{f_1}{f_2} \right )^{0.6}\\ &=\left ( \frac{138}{230} \right )^{1.6} \times \left ( \frac{50}{30} \right )^{0.6} \\ &= (0.6)^{1.6} \times \frac{1}{(0.6)^{0.6}}=0.6\\ \therefore \;\; P_{h2} &=0.6P_{h1} \;\;...(ii) \end{aligned}$$

Given: $\dot{x}(t)=Px+Qu$

$y=Rx$

$$P=\begin{bmatrix} -1 &1 \\ 0& -3 \end{bmatrix}$$,  $$Q=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$,   $$R=\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

For controllability,

$$Q_c=\begin{bmatrix} Q &PQ \end{bmatrix}$$

$$[PQ]=\begin{bmatrix} -1 &1 \\ 0& -3 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 1\\ -3 \end{bmatrix}$$

$$\therefore \;\; Q_c=\begin{bmatrix} 0 &1 \\ 1& -3 \end{bmatrix}$$

Also, for observability,

$$Q_0=\begin{bmatrix} R^T & P^TR^T \end{bmatrix}$$

$$\therefore \;\;Q_0=\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0\\ 1 & -3 \end{bmatrix}$$

$\therefore \;\; |Q_0|=(0 \times -3 -0 \times 1)=0\Rightarrow \;\; non-observable$

Since, $Q_c\neq 0$ and $Q_0=0$

$\therefore$  System is controllable but not observable.

Therefore, the correct answer is **C**.

When $V_0=+V_{sat}$ $V_{UPT}=V_{sat}\times \frac{1k\Omega }{1k\Omega +3k\Omega } = \frac{V_{sat}}{4}$ When, $V_0=-V_{sat}$ $V_{LTP}=V_{sat}\times \frac{1k\Omega }{1k\Omega +1k\Omega }=\frac{-V_{sat}}{2}$ $V_c=V_{final}+(V_{inital}-V_{final})e^{-t/RC}$ In time $t=\Delta t_1$ $V_c=V_{UTP};$ $V_{initial}=V_{LTP};$ $V_{final}=+V_{sat}$ $V_{UTP}=V_{sat}+(V_{LTP}-V_{sat})e^{-\Delta t_1/RC}$ $\frac{V_{sat}}{4}=V_{sat}+\left ( -\frac{V_{sat}}{2}-V_{sat} \right )e^{-\Delta t_1/RC}$ $V_{sat}\left ( -1+\frac{1}{4} \right )=-V_{sat}\left ( \frac{1}{2}+1 \right )e^{-\Delta t_1/RC}$ $\left (1-\frac{1}{4} \right )=\left ( \frac{1}{2}+1 \right )e^{-\Delta t_1/RC}$ $\frac{3}{4}=\frac{3}{2}e^{-\Delta t_1/RC}$ $e^{\Delta t_1/RC}=2\;\;....(i)$ In time $t=\Delta t_2$ $V_c=V_{LTP};$ $V_{initial}=V_{UTP};$ $V_{final}=-V_{sat}$ $V_{LTP}=-V_{sat}+(V_{UTP}+V_{sat})e^{-\Delta t_2/RC}$ $-\frac{V_{sat}}{2}=-V_{sat}+\left ( \frac{V_{sat}}{4}+V_{sat} \right )e^{-\Delta t_2/RC}$ $\left (1-\frac{1}{2} \right )V_{sat}=V_{sat}\left (1+ \frac{1}{4} \right )e^{-\Delta t_2/RC}$ $\frac{1}{2}= \frac{5}{4}e^{-\Delta t_2/RC}$ $e^{\Delta t_2/RC}=\frac{5}{2}\;\;....(ii)$ From equation (i) and (ii), $\frac{e^{\Delta t_1/RC}}{e^{\Delta t_2/RC}}$ $=e^{(\Delta t_1-\Delta t_2)/RC}$ $=\frac{2}{5/2}=\frac{4}{5}=0.8$ Therefore, the correct answer is **1.25** (acceptable range: [1.2, 1.3]).

Using Mason's gain fomlula,

Transfer function,

$G(s)=\frac{C(s)}{U(s)}=\frac{\Sigma P_k\Delta _k}{\Delta }$

Forward paths are:

$P_1=\frac{h_0}{s^2} ,\; P_2=\frac{h_1}{s}$

Individual loops are:

$L_1=\frac{-a_1}{s} , \; L_2=\frac{-a_0}{s^2}$

Non-touching loops=zero

$\therefore \;\;\Delta _1=1,$

$\;\;\;\; \Delta _2=1-\left ( \frac{-a_1}{s} \right ) =\left ( 1+\frac{a_1}{s} \right ) =\left ( \frac{s+a_1}{s} \right )$

$\;\;\;\;\Delta =1-\left ( \frac{-a_1}{s}-\frac{a_0}{s^2} \right )=\frac{s^2+a_1s+a_0}{s^2}$

$\therefore \;\; G(s)=\frac{C(s)}{U(s)}=\frac{P_1\Delta _1+P_2\Delta _2}{\Delta }$

$\;\;\;\;=\frac{\left ( \frac{h_0}{s^2} \right )\times 1+\left ( \frac{h_1}{s} \right )\times \left ( \frac{s+a_1}{s} \right )}{\frac{s^2+a_1s+a_0}{s^2}}$

$\;\;\;=\left [ \frac{h_0+h_1(s+a_1)}{s^2+a_1s+a_0} \right ]$

Given:  $h_1=b_1$ and $h_0=b_0-b_1a_1$

Thus,  $G(s)=\frac{(b_0-b_1a_1)+b_1(s+a_1)}{(s^2+a_1s+a_0)}$

$G(s)=\left ( \frac{b_1s+b_0}{s^2+a_1s+a_0} \right )$

Therefore, the correct answer is **C**.

$$\begin{aligned} x_1&=\left [ 1-\frac{e-1}{e} \right ]=\left [ \frac{e-e+1}{e} \right ]=e^{-1}\\ \text{Also, }x_2&=\left [ x_1-\frac{f(x_1)}{f'(x_1)} \right ]\;\;...(ii)\\ \text{Now, }x_1&=\frac{1}{e}=e^{-1} \text{ and } f(x_1)=(e^{e^{-1}}-1)\\ f'(x_1)&=e^{e^{-1}} \end{aligned}$$

Given $$A=\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1\\ -1&-1 \end{bmatrix},$$ $$B=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 1 \end{bmatrix},$$$$C=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$$

Transfer function of the given system is given by

$\frac{Y(s)}{U(s)}=C(sI-A)^{-1}B$

Now, $$(sI-A)=\begin{bmatrix} s & 0\\ 0 & s \end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1\\ -1&-1 \end{bmatrix}$$

$$\;\;\;=\begin{bmatrix} s & -1\\ 1&s+1 \end{bmatrix}$$

$(sI-A)^{-1}=\frac{1}{|sI-A|}(Adj[A])$

$|sI-A|=s(s+1)+1=(s^2+s+1)$

and $$Adj[A]=\begin{bmatrix} s+1 & 1\\ -1&s \end{bmatrix}$$

$$\therefore \;\;(sI-A)^{-1}=\frac{1}{(s^2+s+1)}\begin{bmatrix} s+1 & 1\\ -1&s \end{bmatrix}$$

$\therefore$ Transfer function,

$$\frac{Y(s)}{U(s)}=\frac{1}{(s^2+s+1)}\left \{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 &0 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} s+1 & 1\\ -1&s \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \right \}$$

$$\;\;=\frac{1}{(s^2+s+1)}\left \{ \begin{bmatrix} (s+1) & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\right \}$$

$\;\;=\frac{1}{(s^2+s+1)} \times 1$

$\frac{Y(s)}{U(s)}=\frac{1}{(s^2+s+1)}$

Given, input=unit step

$\therefore \;\;  U(s)=\frac{1}{s}$

$\therefore \;\; Y(s)=\frac{1}{s}\frac{1}{(s^2+s+1)}=\frac{1}{s(s^2+s+1)}$

$\therefore$ Final Value

$\lim_{s\rightarrow 0}[sY(s)]$

$=\lim_{s\rightarrow 0}\left [ \frac{1}{(s^2+s+1)} \right ]=1$

$\therefore \;\;$ Error=Final value -Initial value

$e_{ss}=0$

Therefore, the correct answer is **A**.

pp:ee:2015:q3.solution_markdown:
Consider a symmetric matrix $$A =\begin{bmatrix} a & b\\ b & d \end{bmatrix}$$

Given $a+d=-6$

$|A|=ad-b^2$

Now since $b^2$ is always non-negative, maximum determinant will come when $b^2=0$.

So we need to maximize

$$\begin{aligned} |A|&=ad-0=ad=a \times -(6+a) \\ &= -a^2-6a\\ \frac{d|A|}{da} &=-2a-6=0 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; a &=-3 \text{ is the only stationary point} \end{aligned}$$

Since, $$\left [\frac{d^2|A|}{da} \right ]_{a=-3}=-2 \lt 0$$, we have a maximum at $a=-3$.

Since $a+d=-6$, corresponding value of $d=-3$.

$|A|=ad=-3 \times -3=9$

Therefore, the correct answer is **9**.

& =e^{-\left(t-t_{0}\right)} \times \int_{-\infty}^{t-t_{0}} e^{\tau} \cdot x(\tau) d \tau

The period of the signal $T$ is the least common multiple (LCM) of the periods of these individual cosine terms. The period of $2\pi t$ (1 Hz) is $T_1 = 1 , \text{sec}$. The period of $4\pi t$ (2 Hz) is $T_2 = 0.5 , \text{sec}$. The period of $6\pi t$ (3 Hz) is $T_3 = \frac{1}{3} , \text{sec}$. The LCM of $T_1, T_2, T_3$ is $T = 1 , \text{sec}$. Step 2: Calculate $|x(t)|^2$ The signal $x(t)$ is real, so we can calculate $|x(t)|^2$ directly: $|x(t)|^2 = (1 + 2 \cos(2\pi t) + 2 \cos(4\pi t) + 2 \cos(6\pi t))^2$ Expanding the square: $|x(t)|^2 = 1 + 4 \cos(2\pi t) + 4 \cos(4\pi t) + 4 \cos(6\pi t) + 4 \cos^2(2\pi t) + 4 \cos(2\pi t) \cos(4\pi t) + \ldots$ Step 3: Integrate over one period We now need to compute the integral of $|x(t)|^2$ over one period $T = 1 , \text{sec}$. Many of the cross-term integrals, like $\int_0^T \cos(2\pi t) \cos(4\pi t) dt$, will be zero due to the orthogonality property of the cosine functions. For the terms that do not vanish: $\int_0^T 1 , dt = T = 1 , \text{sec}$ $\int_0^T \cos^2(2\pi t) , dt = \frac{1}{2} T = \frac{1}{2}$ (using the identity $\cos^2(x) = \frac{1 + \cos(2x)}{2}$) Similarly, $\int_0^T \cos^2(4\pi t) , dt = \frac{1}{2}$ and $\int_0^T \cos^2(6\pi t) , dt = \frac{1}{2}$. Step 4: Sum up the integrals After evaluating the integrals and summing them up, the result of the integral is: $\int_0^T |x(t)|^2 , dt = 1 + 4 \times \frac{1}{2} + 4 \times \frac{1}{2} + 4 \times \frac{1}{2} = 1 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 7$. Step 5: Compute the final result Now, we divide by the period $T = 1] sec: [latex]\frac{1}{T} \int_0^T |x(t)|^2 , dt = \frac{7}{1} = 7$. Final Answer: The value of $\frac{1}{T} \int_0^T |x(t)|^2 , dt$ is closest to 7. Therefore, the correct answer is **7**.

Now check another special case: Case: $n = 2$ Try plugging $n = 2$ directly into the divergence expression: $\nabla \cdot \left( \frac{1}{R^2} \mathbf{a}_R \right) = \frac{1}{R^2} \frac{d}{dR} \left( R^2 \cdot \frac{1}{R^2} \right) = \frac{1}{R^2} \frac{d}{dR} (1) = 0$ So the divergence is zero, which is also independent of $R$. pp:ee:2025:q51.solution_markdown: Step 1: Frequency response $$H(j\omega) = \begin{cases} 1, & |\omega| \leq 200\pi \ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$ Step 2: Find impulse response $h(t)$ by inverse Fourier transform $h(t) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} H(j\omega) e^{j\omega t} d\omega$ But since $H(j\omega) = 1$ for $|\omega| \leq 200\pi$, and 0 otherwise: $h(t) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-200\pi}^{200\pi} e^{j\omega t} d\omega$ Step 3: Evaluate the integral This is a standard Fourier inverse transform result: $h(t) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \cdot \frac{2 \sin(200\pi t)}{t} = \frac{200 \sin(200\pi t)}{\pi t}$ This is the sinc function scaled: $h(t) = 200 \cdot \text{sinc}(200 t)$ where $\text{sinc}(x) = \frac{\sin(\pi x)}{\pi x}$ Step 4: Find $h(0)$ Use the standard limit: $\lim_{t \to 0} \frac{\sin(200\pi t)}{\pi t} = 200$ So: $h(0) = \frac{200 \sin(0)}{\pi \cdot 0} = 200$ Final Answer: 200 Therefore, the correct answer is **200**.

pp:ee:2025:q52.solution_markdown: Step 1: Write the state matrix $$A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \ -2 & -3 \end{bmatrix}$$ Step 2: Find the characteristic equation We compute the determinant of $sI - A$: $$\det(sI - A) = \left| \begin{array}{cc} s & -1 \ 2 & s + 3 \end{array} \right| = s(s + 3) - (-2)(1) = s^2 + 3s + 2$$ Step 3: Find the roots of the characteristic equation $s^2 + 3s + 2 = 0$ Factorizing: $(s + 1)(s + 2) = 0 \Rightarrow s = -1, -2$ Step 4: Compute the sum of the magnitudes of the poles $|{-1}| + |{-2}| = 1 + 2 = 3$ Therefore, the correct answer is **3**.

pp:ee:2025:q53.solution_markdown: Given: Line voltage of motor: $V_L = 4000\ \text{V}$ Apparent power: $S = 390\ \text{kVA}$ Initial power factor: $\cos\phi_1 = 0.77\ (\text{lagging})$ Target power factor: $\cos\phi_2 = 0.85\ (\text{lagging})$ Step 1: Compute the active power (real power) $P = S \cdot \cos\phi_1 = 390 \cdot 0.77 = 300.3\ \text{kW}$ Step 2: Compute reactive power before correction $Q_1 = \sqrt{S^2 - P^2} = \sqrt{390^2 - 300.3^2} = \sqrt{152100 - 90180.09} = \sqrt{61919.91} \approx 248.8\ \text{kVAR}$ Step 3: Compute reactive power after correction New apparent power $S_2 = \frac{P}{\cos\phi_2} = \frac{300.3}{0.85} \approx 353.3\ \text{kVA}$ $Q_2 = \sqrt{S_2^2 - P^2} = \sqrt{353.3^2 - 300.3^2} = \sqrt{124821.89 - 90180.09} = \sqrt{34641.8} \approx 186.0\ \text{kVAR}$ Step 4: Required reactive power by capacitor bank $Q_c = Q_1 - Q_2 = 248.8 - 186.0 = 62.8\ \text{kVAR}$ Step 5: Convert to line current In a 3-phase system, reactive power is: $Q = \sqrt{3} V_L I_L \Rightarrow I_L = \frac{Q}{\sqrt{3} V_L}$ $I_L = \frac{62.8 \times 10^3}{\sqrt{3} \cdot 4000} = \frac{62800}{6928.2} \approx 9.1\ \text{A}$ Final Answer: $\boxed{9.1\ \text{A}}$ Therefore, the correct answer is **9.25** (acceptable range: [8.5, 10]).

pp:ee:2025:q54.solution_markdown: Let’s define: Unit 1 outputs: At 10,000 Rs./MWh → $P_1 = 50\ \text{MW}$ At 10,600 Rs./MWh → $P_1 = 80\ \text{MW}$ Unit 2 outputs: At 10,000 Rs./MWh → $P_2 = 80\ \text{MW}$ At 10,600 Rs./MWh → $P_2 = 92\ \text{MW}$ We are to find outputs at 11,800 Rs./MWh using extrapolation for both units (assuming linearity of power vs incremental cost curve). Step 1: Find slope of output with respect to cost for each unit Unit 1 slope: $\frac{80 - 50}{10,600 - 10,000} = \frac{30}{600} = 0.05\ \text{MW per Rs./MWh}$ Unit 2 slope: $\frac{92 - 80}{10,600 - 10,000} = \frac{12}{600} = 0.02\ \text{MW per Rs./MWh}$ Step 2: Extrapolate to 11,800 Rs./MWh Cost increase: $11,800 - 10,600 = 1,200\ \text{Rs./MWh}$ Unit 1 output: $P_1 = 80 + (0.05)(1200) = 80 + 60 = 140\ \text{MW}$ (but Unit 1 is rated for 100 MW max ⇒ limit to 100 MW) Unit 2 output: $P_2 = 92 + (0.02)(1200) = 92 + 24 = 116\ \text{MW}$ (but Unit 2 is rated for 150 MW ⇒ no limit hit) Step 3: Total Output $P_{\text{total}} = 100 + 116 = \boxed{216\ \text{MW}}$ Final Answer: $\boxed{216}$ Therefore, the correct answer is **216**.

Since $ST \parallel QR$ and $T$ lies on $PR$, by Basic Proportionality Theorem: $\frac{PS}{PQ} = \frac{PT}{PR} = \frac{3}{5}$ So, $PS = \frac{3}{5} \cdot PQ$ Step 2: Area of semicircle is proportional to square of diameter Let the diameter $PQ = d$. Then the area of the semicircle with diameter $PQ$ is: $A_{PQ} = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{\pi d^2}{4} = \frac{\pi d^2}{8}$ Now, $PS = \frac{3}{5} d$, so area of semicircle on PS: $A_{PS} = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{\pi (3d/5)^2}{4} = \frac{\pi d^2}{8} \cdot \frac{9}{25} = A_{PQ} \cdot \frac{9}{25}$ Step 3: Shaded Area = Area of semicircle on PQ − Area of semicircle on PS $A_{\text{shaded}} = A_{PQ} - A_{PS} = A_{PQ} \left(1 - \frac{9}{25}\right) = A_{PQ} \cdot \frac{16}{25}$ Now convert the shaded area as a multiple of the semicircle on PS: $\frac{A_{\text{shaded}}}{A_{PS}} = \frac{A_{PQ} \cdot \frac{16}{25}}{A_{PQ} \cdot \frac{9}{25}} = \frac{16}{9}$ Final Answer: $\boxed{\frac{16}{9}}$ times the area of the semicircle with diameter $PS$ Therefore, the correct answer is **A**.

pp:ee:2026:q8.solution_markdown: Given: A power system has $N$ buses, of which: $P$ are generator buses (including the slack bus) $Q$ are load (PQ) buses Hence, $N=P+Q$ Step 1: Count the unknown voltage angles In the Newton-Raphson load flow method, the voltage angle of the slack bus is known. Therefore, voltage angles of all remaining buses are unknown. $\text{Number of angle unknowns}=N-1$ Step 2: Count the unknown voltage magnitudes Voltage magnitudes are known at generator (PV) buses and at the slack bus. They are unknown only at PQ buses. Therefore, $\text{Number of magnitude unknowns}=Q$ Step 3: Total number of unknowns $(N-1)+Q$ Using $Q=N-P$, $(N-1)+(N-P) = 2N-1-P$ Step 4: Size of the Jacobian matrix The Jacobian matrix is a square matrix whose order equals the total number of unknown variables. Hence, $\text{Jacobian Size} = (2N-1-P)\times(2N-1-P)$ Therefore, the correct answer is **B**.

pp:ee:2026:q9.solution_markdown: Concept: The zero-sequence component of a three-phase set is $V_0=\frac{V_A+V_B+V_C}{3}$ Case-1: The phase voltages are $V_A=V_A\angle\theta_A,\qquad V_B=V_B\angle\theta_B,\qquad V_C=V_C\angle\theta_C$ Therefore, $V_{0,1} = \frac{V_A\angle\theta_A+V_B\angle\theta_B+V_C\angle\theta_C}{3}$ Case-2: Each phasor is rotated by the same angle $\Delta\theta$, while its magnitude remains unchanged. Hence, $V_A'=V_A\angle(\theta_A+\Delta\theta)$ $V_B'=V_B\angle(\theta_B+\Delta\theta)$ $V_C'=V_C\angle(\theta_C+\Delta\theta)$ The new zero-sequence component is $V_{0,2} = \frac{V_A'+V_B'+V_C'}{3}$ Substituting, $V_{0,2} = \frac{ V_A\angle(\theta_A+\Delta\theta) + V_B\angle(\theta_B+\Delta\theta) + V_C\angle(\theta_C+\Delta\theta) }{3}$ Factoring out $e^{j\Delta\theta}$, $V_{0,2} = e^{j\Delta\theta} \frac{ V_A\angle\theta_A + V_B\angle\theta_B + V_C\angle\theta_C }{3}$ $V_{0,2} = e^{j\Delta\theta}V_{0,1}$ Observation: Multiplication by $e^{j\Delta\theta}$ rotates a phasor by $\Delta\theta$ but does not change its magnitude. Therefore, $|V_{0,2}|=|V_{0,1}|$ and $\angle V_{0,2} = \angle V_{0,1} + \Delta\theta$ Hence, the zero-sequence components in the two cases have the same magnitude but different phase angles. Therefore, the correct answer is **D**.

pp:ee:2026:q11.solution_markdown: Concept of Double-Squirrel-Cage Induction Motor A double-squirrel-cage rotor consists of two cages: 1. Outer cage - High resistance - Low reactance 2. Inner cage - Low resistance - High reactance At starting: The slip is $s=1$. Therefore, rotor frequency is maximum, and rotor reactance becomes significant. Since the inner cage has high reactance, its impedance is large: $Z_{\text{inner}} = R_{\text{inner}} + jX_{\text{inner}}$ with $X_{\text{inner}} \gg X_{\text{outer}}$ Hence, most of the rotor current flows through the outer cage, which has lower impedance. The high resistance of the outer cage provides a high starting torque. At rated speed: The slip is very small. Hence rotor frequency is low and rotor reactance becomes negligible. Current distribution is then determined mainly by resistance. Since $R_{\text{inner}} < R_{\text{outer}}$ most of the rotor current flows through the inner cage. Thus the motor behaves like a low-resistance rotor during normal operation, giving good efficiency. The purpose is actually to obtain high effective rotor resistance at starting and low effective rotor resistance during normal running. Therefore, the correct answer is **A**.

pp:ee:2026:q12.solution_markdown: Concept: A synchronous generator connected to an infinite bus operates with: $P=\frac{EV}{X_s}\sin\delta$ where $E$ = internal generated emf, $V$ = infinite-bus voltage, $X_s$ = synchronous reactance, $\delta$ = load angle. Step 1: What happens when field excitation is increased? Increasing field current increases the internal emf $E$ of the generator. Step 2: Real power remains unchanged The mechanical input power is unchanged, and the generator is delivering $P=50\ \text{MW}$ to an infinite bus. Hence, $P=\dfrac{EV}{X_s}\sin\delta$ must remain constant. Since $E$ increases, the quantity $\sin\delta$ must decrease. Therefore, $\delta$ decreases. Step 3: Effect on reactive power and power factor Initially, the generator operates at unity power factor. When excitation is increased, the generator becomes over-excited and supplies reactive power to the system. Thus the stator current leads the terminal voltage. Hence the power factor becomes leading. Step 4: Effect on stator current magnitude Initially, $I_s$ is in phase with $V$ (unity power factor). After over-excitation: Real power component of current remains essentially unchanged. A leading reactive current component appears. Therefore, $|I_s| = \sqrt{I_P^2+I_Q^2}$ increases. So the stator current magnitude increases. Therefore, the correct answer is **C**.

For an ideal cut-set of current sources, KCL must be satisfied. We examine each circuit separately. Circuit-1: Voltage source controlling a voltage source The two voltage sources are connected in parallel. Hence, $V_X=V_D$ But, $V_X=k_1V_D$ Therefore, $k_1V_D=V_D$ For any value of $V_D$, $\boxed{k_1=1}$ Circuit-2: Voltage source controlling a current source An ideal voltage source is connected in parallel with an ideal current source. There is no contradiction. The voltage source fixes the voltage, while the current source fixes the current. Hence, $\boxed{k_2\text{ can have any value}}$ Circuit-3: Current source controlling a voltage source An ideal current source is connected in parallel with an ideal voltage source. Again, there is no contradiction. The current source fixes the current, while the voltage source fixes the voltage. Hence, $\boxed{k_3\text{ can have any value}}$ Circuit-4: Current source controlling a current source The two current sources are connected in parallel. Applying KCL, $I_D+I_X=0$ Given, $I_X=3k_4I_D$ Substituting, $I_D+3k_4I_DI=0$ $(1+3k_4)I_D=0$ For all values of $I_D$, $1+3k_4=0$ $\boxed{k_4=-\frac13}$ Comparing with the options: Only Option (A) satisfies $k_1=1, k_4=-\frac13$ while $k_2$ and $k_3$ can be arbitrary. pp:ee:2026:q19.solution_markdown: Concept: The slope of the asymptotic Bode magnitude plot helps identify the poles and zeros of the transfer function. Step 1: Observe the low-frequency behavior The magnitude plot has a slope of $-20\ \text{dB/decade}$ for frequencies below $\omega_0.$ A slope of $-20\ \text{dB/decade}$ indicates the presence of a pole at the origin. Thus, the transfer function contains the factor $\frac{1}{s/\omega_0}.$ Step 2: Observe the break frequency At $\omega=\omega_0,$ the slope changes from $-20\ \text{dB/decade} \] to [latex] 0\ \text{dB/decade}.$ A change in slope of $+20\ \text{dB/decade}$ indicates the presence of a zero at $\omega=\omega_0.$ Hence, the transfer function also contains the factor $1+\frac{s}{\omega_0}.$ Step 3: Form the transfer function Combining the pole at the origin and the zero at $\omega_0,$ we obtain $G(s) = \frac{1+\dfrac{s}{\omega_0}} {\dfrac{s}{\omega_0}}.$ Verification: For $\omega \ll \omega_0,$ $G(j\omega)\approx\frac{1}{j\omega/\omega_0},$ which gives a slope of $-20\ \text{dB/decade}.$ For $\omega \gg \omega_0,$ $G(j\omega)\approx \frac{j\omega/\omega_0}{j\omega/\omega_0}=1,$ so the magnitude becomes $0\ \text{dB},$ which matches the given Bode plot. Therefore, the correct transfer function is $\boxed{G(s)=\frac{1+\dfrac{s}{\omega_0}}{\dfrac{s}{\omega_0}}}$ Therefore, the correct answer is **A**.

A periodic function is formed as $f(x)=\sum_{m=-\infty}^{\infty}g(x+2\pi m),$ which is a periodic function with period $2\pi.$ Step 1: Identify the symmetry Since $f(-x)=-f(x),$ the function is odd. Hence,
  • All cosine coefficients are zero.
  • Only sine coefficients are present.
Therefore, $a_n=0.$ Step 2: Calculate the sine coefficients The sine coefficient is $b_n=\dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}f(x)\sin(nx)\,dx.$ Substituting the given waveform, $b_n = \dfrac{1}{\pi} \left[ \int_{-\pi}^{0}(-k)\sin(nx)\,dx + \int_{0}^{\pi}k\sin(nx)\,dx \right].$ Since the two integrals are equal, $b_n = \dfrac{2k}{\pi} \int_{0}^{\pi}\sin(nx)\,dx.$ Now, $\int_{0}^{\pi}\sin(nx)\,dx = \dfrac{1-(-1)^n}{n}.$ Hence, $b_n = \dfrac{2k}{n\pi} \left(1-(-1)^n\right).$ For odd harmonics, $(-1)^n=-1,$ therefore, $b_n=\dfrac{4k}{n\pi}.$ Step 3: Third harmonic For $n=3,$ $a_3=0,$ and $b_3=\dfrac{4k}{3\pi}.$ The question states that the sum of the third-harmonic cosine and sine coefficients is $a_3+b_3=\dfrac{2}{3\pi}.$ Since $a_3=0,$ $\dfrac{4k}{3\pi} = \dfrac{2}{3\pi}.$ Therefore, $4k=2$ $k=\dfrac{1}{2}.$ Therefore, the correct answer is **B**.

$I_A'=\dfrac{I_A}{60},\qquad

The auxiliary transformer has a turns ratio of

$2:1$

Since current is inversely proportional to turns,

$\dfrac{I_s}{I_p}=2$

Thus, the delta-side current is twice the CT secondary current.

For the $Yn\Delta$ auxiliary transformer, the current supplied to the R-phase burden is

$I_{AR}=\dfrac{2}{60}(I_A-I_B)$

Now,

$I_A-I_B=(572.812+j50.115)-(-254.525-j459.175)$

$=827.337+j509.290$

Therefore,

$I_{AR}=\dfrac{2}{60}(827.337+j509.290)

=27.578+j16.976~\text{A}$

Because of the delta connection, the burden branch current is

$I_{AR}=8.932+j0.641~\text{A}$

Magnitude:

$|I_{AR}|=\sqrt{8.932^2+0.641^2}=8.954~\text{A}$

Phase angle:

$\angle I_{AR}

=\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{0.641}{8.932}\right)

=4.105^\circ$

Hence,

pp:ee:2026:q30.concept_summary: Power Systems - Switch Gear and Protection
pp:ee:2026:q30.solution_markdown:
The operating characteristic of the reactance relay is

$X \leq 1~\Omega$

where $X$ is the reactance seen by the relay.

The impedance seen by the relay is

$Z=R+jX$

The corresponding admittance is

$Y=\dfrac{1}{Z}=G+jB$

where

$G=\dfrac{R}{R^2+X^2},

\qquad

B=-\dfrac{X}{R^2+X^2}$

Since

$R=\dfrac{G}{G^2+B^2},

\qquad

X=-\dfrac{B}{G^2+B^2}$

substitute into the relay characteristic

$X\le 1$

to obtain

$-\dfrac{B}{G^2+B^2}\le 1$

Rearranging,

$G^2+B^2+B\ge 0$

Completing the square,

$G^2+\left(B+\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2\ge\dfrac14$

Multiplying both sides by 4,

$4G^2+4\left(B+\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2\ge 1$

or

$4G^2+(2B+1)^2\ge 1$

Hence,

$G^2+\left(B+\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2\ge\dfrac{1}{4}$

Therefore, the correct answer is **A**.

pp:ee:2026:q31.solution_markdown:
The transformer has a voltage transformation ratio

$\dfrac{V_P}{V_S}=0.866+j0.5$

Let

$a=0.866+j0.5$

The leakage impedance referred to the secondary side is

$y \text{ p.u.}$

,where $y$ is the series admittance.

For a transformer having an off-nominal complex tap ratio $a$, the branch equations are

$I_P=\dfrac{y}{|a|^2}V_P-\dfrac{y}{a^*}V_S$

$I_S=-\dfrac{y}{a}V_P+yV_S$

where $a^*$ is the complex conjugate of $a$.

Since

$a=0.866+j0.5,

\qquad

|a|=\sqrt{0.866^2+0.5^2}=1$

therefore,

$|a|^2=1$

Also,

$a^*=0.866-j0.5$

Since $|a|=1$,

$\dfrac{1}{a}=a^*=0.866-j0.5$

and

$\dfrac{1}{a^*}=a=0.866+j0.5$

Substituting these values,

$I_P

=

yV_P

-

\dfrac{y}{0.866-j0.5}V_S$

and

$I_S

=

-\dfrac{y}{0.866+j0.5}V_P

+yV_S$

Hence, the Y-bus representation is

$$\begin{bmatrix}

I_P\\

I_S

\end{bmatrix}

=

\begin{bmatrix}

y & -\dfrac{y}{0.866-j0.5}\\[8pt]

-\dfrac{y}{0.866+j0.5} & y

\end{bmatrix}

\begin{bmatrix}

V_P\\

V_S

\end{bmatrix}$$

Therefore, the correct answer is **D**.

pp:ee:2026:q32.concept_summary: Electric Circuits - Steady state AC Analysis
pp:ee:2026:q32.solution_markdown:
The instantaneous power is

$p=vi

\;=\;

V_mI_m\sin(\omega t)\sin(\omega t-\theta)$

Using the trigonometric identity

$\sin A\sin B=\dfrac{1}{2}\left[\cos(A-B)-\cos(A+B)\right],$

we get

$p

=

\dfrac{V_mI_m}{2}

\left[

\cos\theta

-

\cos(2\omega t-\theta)

\right]$

The average power over one half-cycle is

$P_{\text{avg}}

=

\dfrac{1}{T/2}

\int_{0}^{T/2}

p\,dt$

Substituting the expression for $p$,

$P_{\text{avg}}

=

\dfrac{1}{T/2}

\int_{0}^{T/2}

\dfrac{V_mI_m}{2}

\left[

\cos\theta

-

\cos(2\omega t-\theta)

\right]dt$

Separating the two terms,

$P_{\text{avg}}

=

\dfrac{V_mI_m}{T}

\left[

\cos\theta

\int_{0}^{T/2}dt

-

\int_{0}^{T/2}\cos(2\omega t-\theta)\,dt

\right]$

The first integral is

$\int_{0}^{T/2}dt=\dfrac{T}{2}$

For the second integral,

$\int_{0}^{T/2}\cos(2\omega t-\theta)\,dt

=

\dfrac{1}{2\omega}

\left[

\sin(2\omega t-\theta)

\right]_{0}^{T/2}$

Since

$\omega T=2\pi,$

we have

$2\omega\left(\dfrac{T}{2}\right)=2\pi$

Therefore,

$\sin(2\pi-\theta)=\sin(-\theta),$

and hence

$\left[

\sin(2\omega t-\theta)

\right]_{0}^{T/2}

=

\sin(-\theta)-\sin(-\theta)=0$

Thus, the second integral is zero.

Hence,

$P_{\text{avg}}

=

\dfrac{V_mI_m}{T}

\left(

\cos\theta\cdot\dfrac{T}{2}

\right)$

$P_{\text{avg}}

=

\dfrac{V_mI_m}{2}\cos\theta$

Therefore, the correct answer is **C**.

pp:ee:2026:q33.concept_summary: Electric Circuits - Transients and Steady State Response
pp:ee:2026:q33.solution_markdown:
Before $t=0$, the current source is OFF since

$i_s=1u(t)\ \text{mA}.$

Hence, for $t<0$, the circuit is in DC steady state and the capacitor behaves as an open circuit.

Step 1: Capacitor voltage at $t=0^-$

The capacitor voltage is obtained using the voltage divider formed by $25~\text{k}\Omega$ and $100~\text{k}\Omega$.

$V_C(0^-)

=

10\left(\frac{100}{25+100}\right)

=

8~\text{V}$

Since the voltage across a capacitor cannot change instantaneously,

$V_C(0^+)=V_C(0^-)=8~\text{V}$

Step 2: Final value $t\rightarrow\infty$

For $t>0$, the current source supplies

$1~\text{mA}.$

At steady state, the capacitor again behaves as an open circuit.

Applying KCL at the capacitor node,

$\frac{V-10}{25\,000}

+

\frac{V}{100\,000}

=

1\times10^{-3}$

Multiplying throughout by $100\,000$,

$4(V-10)+V=100$

$5V=140$

$V=28~\text{V}$

Hence,

$V_C(\infty)=28~\text{V}$

Step 3: Time constant

To determine the time constant, deactivate all independent sources.

Replace the 10 V source by a short circuit.

Replace the 1 mA current source by an open circuit.

The resistance seen by the capacitor is

$R_{th}

=

25~\text{k}\Omega

\parallel

100~\text{k}\Omega

=

20~\text{k}\Omega$

Therefore,

$\tau

=

R_{th}C

=

20\times10^3

\times

10\times10^{-6}

=

0.2~\text{s}$

Step 4: Capacitor voltage at $t=0.5~\text{s}$

The capacitor voltage is

$V_C(t)

=

V_f

+

(V_i-V_f)e^{-t/\tau}$

where

$V_i=8~\text{V},

\qquad

V_f=28~\text{V}.$

Thus,

$V_C(0.5)

=

28+(8-28)e^{-0.5/0.2}$

Since

$e^{-2.5}\approx0.0821,$

we get

$V_C(0.5)

=

28-20(0.0821)

=

26.36~\text{V}$

Hence,

$V_C(0^+)=8.00~\text{V},

\qquad

V_C(0.5)=26.36~\text{V},

\qquad

V_C(\infty)=28.00~\text{V}$

Therefore, the correct answer is **B**.

pp:ee:2026:q51.solution_markdown:
Diode conducts when $v_s > V_{dc}$:

$100\sin\theta > 50 \Rightarrow \sin\theta > 0.5 \Rightarrow \theta \in [\pi/6,\ 5\pi/6]$

Conducting current: $i = \dfrac{v_s - V_{dc}}{R} = \dfrac{100\sin\theta - 50}{10}$

Average current:

$I_{avg} = \dfrac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\pi/6}^{5\pi/6}\dfrac{100\sin\theta - 50}{10}\,d\theta$

$= \dfrac{1}{2\pi}\left[-10\cos\theta - 5\theta\right]_{\pi/6}^{5\pi/6}$

$= \dfrac{1}{2\pi}\left[\left(-10\times(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) - \frac{25\pi}{6}\right) - \left(-10\times\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} - \frac{5\pi}{6}\right)\right]$

$= \dfrac{1}{2\pi}\left[10\sqrt{3} - \frac{20\pi}{6}\right] = \dfrac{5\sqrt{3}}{\pi} - \dfrac{5}{3} \approx 2.756 - 1.667 \approx 1.09$ A

Therefore, the correct answer is **1.09** (acceptable range: [1.04, 1.14]).

pp:ee:2026:q52.solution_markdown: Contour $C$: center $2+i$, radius $1.5$. Check singularities: $z = i$: distance from center $= |2+i-i| = 2 > 1.5 \rightarrow$ outside $z = 2$: distance from center $= |2-(2+i)| = 1 < 1.5 \rightarrow$ inside By Residue Theorem: $\oint = 2\pi i \times \text{Res}_{z=2}\dfrac{(z+1)^2}{(z-i)(z-2)}$ $\text{Res}_{z=2} = \dfrac{(2+1)^2}{(2-i)} = \dfrac{9}{2-i} = \dfrac{9(2+i)}{5} = \dfrac{18+9i}{5}$ $\oint = 2\pi i \times \dfrac{18+9i}{5} = \dfrac{2\pi(-9+18i)}{5}$ $\left|\oint\right| = \dfrac{2\pi}{5}\sqrt{81+324} = \dfrac{2\pi}{5}\times\sqrt{405} = \dfrac{2\pi \times 9\sqrt{5}}{5} = \dfrac{18\pi}{\sqrt{5}} \approx 25.29$ Therefore, the correct answer is **25.3** (acceptable range: [25, 25.6]).

pp:ee:2026:q53.solution_markdown: Total sphere charge: $Q_{vol} = \rho_v \times \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3 = \dfrac{3}{\pi} \times 10^{-6} \times \dfrac{4\pi}{3}(2)^3 = 32 \times 10^{-6}$ C Point charge: $q = \pi \times 8.854 \times 10^{-12}$ C Distances from origin (both points outside sphere $r=2$): $r_1 = \sqrt{9+0+16} = 5$ m (start) $r_2 = \sqrt{0+0+16} = 4$ m (end) Work done: $W = q(V_2 - V_1) = q \times \dfrac{Q_{vol}}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\left(\dfrac{1}{r_2} - \dfrac{1}{r_1}\right)$ $= \pi \times 8.854 \times 10^{-12} \times \dfrac{32 \times 10^{-6}}{4\pi \times 8.854 \times 10^{-12}}\left(\dfrac{1}{4} - \dfrac{1}{5}\right)$ $= \dfrac{32 \times 10^{-6}}{4} \times \dfrac{1}{20} = 8 \times 10^{-6} \times 0.05 = 4 \times 10^{-7}$ J $= 0.40\ \mu$J Therefore, the correct answer is **0.4** (acceptable range: [0.38, 0.42]).

pp:ee:2026:q54.solution_markdown: Expand the objective: $f(\alpha) = E\left((X - \alpha Y)^2\right) = E(X^2) - 2\alpha E(XY) + \alpha^2 E(Y^2)$ $= 4 - 2\alpha(0.9) + 9\alpha^2$ $= 9\alpha^2 - 1.8\alpha + 4$ Minimise by differentiating and setting to zero: $\dfrac{df}{d\alpha} = 18\alpha - 1.8 = 0$ $\alpha = \dfrac{1.8}{18} = 0.1$ Answer: 0.1 Therefore, the correct answer is **0.1**.

pp:ee:2026:q55.solution_markdown: Let $I = \dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{\infty}\dfrac{x^n}{(1+x^n)(1+x^2)}dx$ where $n = 2026$. Also define: $J = \dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{\infty}\dfrac{1}{(1+x^n)(1+x^2)}dx$ Step 1: $I + J = \dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{\infty}\dfrac{1}{1+x^2}dx = \dfrac{1}{\pi} \times \dfrac{\pi}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}$ Step 2: Substitute $x \to 1/x$ in $I$: $I = \dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{\infty}\dfrac{x^{-n}}{(1+x^{-n})(1+x^{-2})}\dfrac{dx}{x^2} = \dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{\infty}\dfrac{1}{(x^n+1)(1+x^2)}dx = J$ Step 3: Since $I = J$: $2I = \dfrac{1}{2} \Rightarrow I = \dfrac{1}{4} = 0.25$ Answer: 0.25 Therefore, the correct answer is **0.25**.

Set equal: $x^{2} = -x^{2} - 2x - 1$

Discriminant $= (2)^{2} - 4(2)(1) = 4 - 8 = -4 < 0$

No real solutions -> curves do not intersect.

Note: $-x^{2}-2x-1 = -(x+1)^{2} \leq 0$ and $x^{2} \geq 0$, so they only meet if both sides = 0 simultaneously, which is impossible.

Therefore, the correct answer is **A**.
